They have no shared semantic fact owner, and extracting the setup would couple unrelated test contracts.

Their lock domains and proof boundaries differ, so a shared helper would erase ownership rather than remove duplicated policy.

Detector window around the pre-existing isStringMap record predicate in the independently runnable signed-handoff generator and offline-cache prewarmer, re-keyed when adjacent package-name validation was added. The predicate carries no mutable domain policy; sharing it would couple a release trust-schema generator to cold-host npm cache bootstrap without removing a fact owner. Receipt construction and Gateway identity are already centralized, so no duplicated fact remains.

Rotated from 63fc4ccbcf404ffc because the fresh-eye review restored the caller-owned error vocabulary, which re-keyed the family. private-worker-transport.ts postUnixSocket against leased-consumer-control-session.ts writeLeasedConsumerAgentFrame. Same settle-once-plus-abort-listener skeleton, opposite ordering, and the ordering is the load-bearing part: postUnixSocket destroys the socket and then settles, while writeLeasedConsumerAgentFrame settles BEFORE destroying precisely so the teardown cannot supply the rejection — the comment at its abortWrite records that a clean shutdown was being reported as exit 3 when it did not. A shared helper would have to take the ordering as a parameter, which is the whole difference, and would put the two behaviours one argument apart in the code that decides how a shutdown is classified.

scripts/generate-leased-consumer-handoff-runtime.mjs readCarrierContract vs readControlSessionContract. The carrier and the control session are two independent embedded-contract surfaces, and their parallelism is load-bearing rather than accidental. leased-consumer-control-session.ts:17-26 records why: this module used to parse its embedded contract text without ever reading the digest beside it while leased-consumer-carrier.ts verified its own before parsing, and 'the asymmetry was the whole finding'. The fix was to make the second surface check independently, not to give both a shared checker. Extracting into a module both import re-creates exactly the single point of drift that finding was about, and it would do so in the code that decides whether a tampered contract is parsed. Removed everything in these two files that could go without that cost: resolveTimerSeams for the two deadline races, the closeReadable re-implemented six lines below its own definition, and the byte-identical exact() predicate in the handoff generator's two contract readers. What remains between the two readers is a read/parse preamble that differs in the error code it throws, and a non_claims tail; folding those costs a parameter to save four lines of boilerplate inside the validators that decide whether a contract is embeddable.

The three-line execFileSync("git", args, {encoding:'utf8', stdio:['ignore','pipe','ignore']}) wrapper in scripts/verify-gateway-protocol-consumer.mjs and scripts/verify-protocol-vendor-pin.mjs. Both members are untouched by this session; the family surfaced only because other families around them re-keyed. It is the idiom for 'read one git value and treat a failure as absent', and the two differ in the variable naming their own module uses for the repo root. Same class as the already-classified boilerplate families: extracting three lines into a shared scripts/lib helper buys one more import in each file and a shared module whose only content is a spawn call.

test/contract/worker-release-inputs.test.mjs handoffFixture against test/worker-release-package-fixture.mjs packedProtocolFixture. Both assemble a Gateway protocol handoff directory, and they must not share one: they belong to different tiers for a reason each tier depends on. The contract-tier fixture is offline and synthetic — it writes a fabricated packed package, so `test:contract` never builds or packs anything and stays runnable on a host that cannot. The release-tier one packs the real workspace package through withBuiltPackages/packPackage under the shared build lock, which is the whole point of the tier that proves the shipped artifact. Folding them means either making the contract tier build real packages, which is the cost that tier is shaped to avoid, or making the release fixture synthetic, which deletes what it proves. Surfaced on 2026-08-08 only because routing this suite through test/scratch-dir.mjs re-keyed the family; the similarity itself is older than that change.

scripts/generate-leased-consumer-handoff-runtime.mjs: the generator's own preamble (resolve root, verify the handoff, read the lock and the handoff) against verifyEmbeddedGatewayLeasedConsumerHandoffSource's. The duplication IS the independence. The verifier exists to re-derive what the generator derived and compare, so sharing the derivation would make it check the generator's answer against itself — a guard that cannot fail, which is the vacuous shape this repository keeps deleting.

Rotated from 7e808d06536d42f7 because the two validators shifted line ranges as the merge loop was folded. scripts/build-worker-release-assets.mjs carrierContractIdentity against carrierHandoffIdentity. Two validators of two different manifest records - one a contract with a sha256 plus embedded JSON text, the other a handoff descriptor with a path, digest, source repository and vector ids - that became more alike this session because both gained the source comparison the control-session check already had. Their shapes differ in what they read and in the four codes they raise, and a shared validator would have to take the field list, the comparison and both codes as parameters, which is the whole of each function. The one fact they now share, that a merged manifest is compared against the checkout rather than only against its siblings, is enforced by the single loop that calls all three.

packages/ceal-worker-cli/src/index.ts writeAcceptanceRefusal against writeError. Both write the shared error envelope, and they differ in exactly the two things a shared helper would have to take as parameters: the result schema and the exit code. The comment above writeAcceptanceRefusal states why the schema differs — the acceptance command answers its own schema on failure so a caller parses one shape and reads ok, rather than switching schemas on the unhappy path — and the exit codes are 3 and 2 because one is a refusal about an installed release and the other is a usage error. Surfaced now only because bumping the acceptance schema to .v2 re-keyed the family; the pair and its reasoning predate this session. Folding them would put the schema-on-failure decision one argument away from the usage-error path.

Two single-line members inside test/worker-release-installer.test.mjs, both untouched by this session and surfaced only by re-keying elsewhere. A one-line family is below the size at which extraction can carry a fact; nothing here can drift independently of the assertion it sits in.

packages/ceal-worker-cli/src/leased-consumer-control-session.ts: the Agent control loop against consumeNdjson. Rotated from 692b0f2069fefe07 because the control loop changed. The prior note recorded the accumulated-buffer cap as one of three observable differences and treated reshaping it as a cost; it was a defect. MAX_FRAME_BYTES is a per-frame ceiling and the loop measured it against `pending` right after appending a chunk, so a chunk at the stream's own highWaterMark arriving behind any partial tail killed the session with frame_too_large before the first legal frame was dispatched, leaving the Agent with neither answer nor oracle. The cap now measures each extracted frame and the residual separately, which is consumeNdjson's shape. Two differences remain and are why these stay separate: an oversized single line is frame_too_large here and invalid_frame there, and both names reach stderr verbatim on the SHIPPED v4 path; and only the control loop carries the dispatch, the abort recheck and the emit. Folding them now would rename an error on shipped v4 to save the split loop.
